video_title: EIP-8363: Should ETH Be Sound Money or a Productive Asset?
gist: A live debate on EIP-8363, the Ethereum issuance proposal that burns a rising share of validator rewards as the staking ratio climbs, driving staking yield toward zero near 50% of ETH staked. EIP co-author Jerome (Ethereum Foundation / Ethereum France) argues over-staking is an unnecessary subsidy paid via dilution and that the window for a smooth transition closes as ETH approaches 50% staked by 2028; DV Labs CEO Oshene counters that Ethereum's real security is roughly $5M/day (not $100B) and that cutting issuance below a 0.5% floor invites censorship and stake concentration; Kevin (Gitcoin founder, undecided) frames it as a political-economy fight between ultrasound money and productive-asset camps that all core devs must resolve at ACD 185 and the October 26 inclusion decision.

insights.claim: EIP-8363 would burn a rising portion of validator rewards as Ethereum's staking ratio climbs, so issuance-funded staking yield falls toward zero at roughly 50% of ETH staked, replacing the current curve that never switches off the incentive to stake.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: If adopted, the marginal ETH staking yield becomes a decreasing function of participation — every staking-yield-dependent business model needs to be re-underwritten against a falling, ratio-dependent curve rather than a fixed rate.
insights.quote: a burn that grows with the staking ratio. So uh the reward sters towards zero uh at around the level of half the EA at stake

insights.claim: The EIP-8363 curve is anchored on roughly four to five years of research concluding Ethereum's minimum viable issuance for economic security is about 0.5% per year, with the curve's maximum payout targeted at a 20-30% staking ratio.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: The 0.5% figure is the negotiating anchor — both sides accept it as the security floor, so the entire fight is about whether the curve is allowed to go below it.
insights.quote: the minimum viable issuance of Ethereum should be around.5%

insights.claim: The proposal deliberately avoids a cliff: between the current discussion and full force there would be roughly 18 months to two years of transition after go-live, plus lead time before an implementation date is fixed.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Any DeFi unwind would be gradual, not a single repricing event — the trade is a multi-year drift in ETH staking yield, not a gap-down.

insights.claim: The curve was explicitly designed so Ethereum never crosses 50% of ETH at stake, because the protocol's proof-of-stake security and credible neutrality were not designed for staking above that level.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: The 50% ceiling is the design constraint driving the whole proposal — watch whether critics can move the EF off it, since accepting a 0.5% floor implies accepting staking ratios above 50%.
insights.quote: we did not design our security and our proof of stake for uh staking above 50%. Uh our credible neutrality is in question here.

insights.claim: Jerome projects post-EIP equilibrium at roughly 40-45% of ETH staked, while Oshene's read of the same research puts it at 45-49%, implying issuance-based yield of about 0.3% APR at a 45% ratio.
insights.speaker: Jerome and Oshene
insights.so_what: Both camps converge on ~0.3% APR as the post-EIP steady state, roughly a 10x cut from today's ~3% — that number is the input for any DeFi looping, LST, or ETH-treasury cash-flow model.
insights.quote: I've been digging into the research on your EIP and mine is 45 to 49.

insights.claim: A widely circulated criticism that stakers would be taxed on gross rewards while the burn eats their profit rests on a misreading: like EIP-1559 burns, the burned portion never reaches the validator's withdrawable balance.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: The 'up to 77% after-tax income drop' headline for home validators is overstated on the mechanics; the real tax problem is structural, not created by this EIP.
insights.quote: it's it's not we give you one and then we take five. Uh you the one never really reach your activable balance.

insights.claim: Ethereum's practically relevant security is not the tens of billions of staked ETH but roughly $5 million per day at the current issuance curve, and could fall to about $1 million a day or less under the proposed curve.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Reframes the ETH security narrative from a $100B+ headline to a daily bribery cost comparable to a mid-size hedge fund's P&L — a bear input for anyone underwriting Ethereum as trillion-dollar settlement infrastructure.
insights.quote: We don't really have hundred billion dollars of security. We really have five million a day at the current curve.

insights.claim: Ethereum has two distinct security properties — the cost to revert finality and the cost to censor transactions — and EIP-8363's economic-security reasoning only addresses the first, because a 51% coalition that refuses to attest to blocks containing disfavored transactions pays no protocol penalty.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating Ethereum's neutrality premium should track the censorship-cost metric separately from staked value; issuance policy does almost nothing for it.
insights.quote: if they do that, um, there's no penalty. So long as there's 51% of them or more doing it, um, it costs them nothing.

insights.claim: The EIP's own author concedes the cost to bribe or coerce validators into censoring is only a couple of million dollars a day and calls that low for a network aiming to settle the world, but argues DVT and FOCIL — not issuance — are the right tools for that layer.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: A rare on-record concession from the EF side that censorship cost is cheap — it shifts the burden onto the DVT/FOCIL roadmap delivering, which is a dependency worth tracking.

insights.claim: Oshene's core attack scenario is that an unnamed entity holding 40-60% of staked ETH could push issuance to zero under the new curve, forcing rational smaller stakers to exit and leaving that entity in control of the majority of stake.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: A zero-floor curve creates a griefing vector where a large staker can economically evict competitors — the strongest technical objection to watch in the all core devs debate.
insights.quote: an entity that has 40 50 60% of ETH, which I won't name, um, could just drive the issuance to zero and it would cause pretty much everybody else that's a rational actor to leave

insights.claim: Oshene states he would find the proposal far less objectionable if issuance stopped at the 0.5% research floor rather than trending to zero, identifying the specific amendment most likely to unblock consensus.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: A 0.5% floor is the concrete compromise on the table — if it appears in a revised EIP, opposition likely collapses and the DeFi cascade fears shrink materially.
insights.quote: I think if we stopped at 0.5% issuance and didn't cut it any lower, this would be a much like less objectionable proposal.

insights.claim: Oshene argues Ethereum's 1% issuance is lower than almost everything else in the world and is good for security, framing the debate as ultrasound money versus crypto security principles rather than money versus yield.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: The opposition is not purely commercial — a technically credible camp is defending tail emissions on security grounds, which makes the EIP harder to pass than a simple business-lobby fight.
insights.quote: I think it's less um ultrasound money versus productive asset.

insights.claim: Oshene compares a zero-issuance Ethereum to Bitcoin's security-budget crisis and notes that chains which are more centralized trade at roughly a tenth of Ethereum's value, arguing security should not be traded for slightly harder money.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Directly disputes the assumption that lower issuance mechanically raises ETH's price — the valuation argument runs through security, not scarcity.
insights.quote: I think we shouldn't give up Ethereum security lightly um under the assumption that like slightly harder money would would make the price go up

insights.claim: Across five or six large mature proof-of-stake chains most have no slashing at all, the highest sit around 70% staked and many at ~50%, while Ethereum has taken nearly six years to reach roughly 36%.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Cross-chain base rates suggest Ethereum's climb past 50% is slower and less certain than the EIP's urgency implies, weakening the 'act now' case.

insights.claim: Neither side believes the debate touches Ethereum's supply integrity — printing extra ETH or changing balances is enforced by full-node operators and would be visible immediately, so only finality reversion and censorship are genuinely at stake.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Useful boundary for risk assessment: the issuance fight is a security-economics and governance question, not a supply-inflation risk to ETH holders.

insights.claim: Aave's Stani Kulechov calculated that EIP-8363 would cut validator income from roughly 3% to 1.5%, a 50% reduction, and argued it could accelerate the very staking capture the EIP claims to deter.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin), citing Stani
insights.so_what: Halved validator income is the number DeFi lending and looping desks are modelling; it directly compresses LST yields that underpin ETH-collateralized credit.
insights.quote: Stani from A said he ran the math and if validator income falls from about 3% down to 1.5% that's a 50% cut.

insights.claim: SharpLink's Joe Shalom published a critique headlined that the proposal would undermine DeFi and that DeFi is Ethereum's superpower, and Bankless co-founder Ryan Sean Adams called the EIP dead in the water.
insights.speaker: host (Laura Shin) and Kevin
insights.so_what: Names the specific opposition coalition — ETH treasury companies, lending protocols, and media — whose public positioning is the best real-time gauge of whether the EIP advances.
insights.quote: it would undermine DeFi and DeFi is Ethereum's superpower

insights.claim: The EIP's authors admit they have no cascade model for the DeFi knock-on effects and are inviting affected venues to co-build one, meaning the proposal is being debated without a quantified impact study.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: The absence of Monte Carlo or cascade analysis is itself a reason core devs may defer — and an opening for Gauntlet-style analytics firms to shape the outcome.
insights.quote: we don't have a cascade model. We know that this will have an impact.

insights.claim: Jerome argues that heavy ETH borrowing demand in lending markets, viewed as a repo market, is largely people shorting ETH, so tapering the borrowing case for ETH is good for the asset rather than harmful.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard 'this kills ETH borrow demand' objection — if the EF genuinely reads borrow demand as short interest, expect little sympathy for lending-protocol complaints.

insights.claim: Jerome dismisses TVL as a vanity metric that double-counts the same ETH looped through derivatives, arguing transaction volume and position churn — which actually burn ETH — are the real activity measure.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: If EF thinking shifts from TVL to fee-burning volume, protocols marketed on TVL lose narrative standing in Ethereum governance — a reason to reweight DeFi analytics toward volume and burn.
insights.quote: what matters is the volume what matters is how much transaction is being done

insights.claim: Jerome rejects the argument that businesses built on ETH staking yield have a claim against changing it, noting Ethereum has repeatedly modified its issuance policy — always downward — and that consensus changes were already telegraphed with Lean Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Signals the EF will not treat existing yield-dependent business models as a veto — a durable policy risk for any ETH staking-yield business.

insights.claim: Jerome characterizes leveraged looping — borrowing ETH against stablecoins to farm staking yield — as earning on other ETH holders' dilution while buying Ethereum no extra security, and therefore not worth subsidizing.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Looping strategies are explicitly the target of the EIP; leveraged ETH staking carries protocol-policy risk on top of market risk.

insights.claim: SharpLink publicly opposed the issuance change on productive-asset grounds, then announced a Galaxy DeFi fund focused on staking the next day and $200 million of ETH sent to Lido the day after.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that the loudest opponents have direct book exposure — treat their public analysis as positioning, and watch ETH treasury companies' Lido flows as the revealed preference.

insights.claim: The opposition is concentrated among Ethereum's business constituency rather than its developers, repeating the business-versus-devs split that Laura Shin documented from Ethereum's founding and sees recur across crypto.
insights.speaker: host (Laura Shin)
insights.so_what: A useful lens for predicting crypto governance outcomes: when the split is devs vs businesses, technical process usually decides, and business pressure alone rarely kills a proposal outright.

themes.theme: Governance mechanics and the decision calendar

insights.claim: Kevin frames ETH issuance as a political economy problem rather than an engineering one, with no single right answer and two tribes that have not moved toward each other in roughly two years of debate.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin)
insights.so_what: Explains why technical arguments will not resolve this — the outcome hinges on who holds legitimacy in off-chain governance, not on better modeling.
insights.quote: This is not an engineering problem. This is a political economy problem.

insights.claim: All core devs meeting number 185 was scheduled for Thursday August 20th at 1400 UTC as the first venue where EIP-8363's contentiousness comes to a head.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin)
insights.so_what: A dated, tradeable catalyst for ETH and for LST/staking-linked assets — the call's outcome is the near-term signal on whether the yield cut advances.
insights.quote: all core developers meeting number 185 is scheduled for Thursday August 20th at 1400 UTC

insights.claim: Jerome identifies October 26th as the harder deadline: the date core devs decide whether proposals currently at 'proposed for inclusion' status — including EIP-8363 and an anti-correlation penalties EIP — are mature enough for inclusion, triggering testnets.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: The real go/no-go date to diary; inclusion at that point would start the clock on the 18-month-plus transition and repricing of ETH staking yield.

insights.claim: Roughly 66 EIPs were proposed for the next hard fork and Jerome's expected outcome for the August call is neither adoption nor rejection but continued discussion, with the likely resolution deferred to a later all core devs meeting.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Base case is no decision in August — expect headline risk without resolution, and avoid trading the ACD date as if it were binary.

insights.claim: Ethereum forks roughly every six months, so missing the next fork later this year would push EIP-8363 to a fork in early or first-half 2027, and Kevin argues that missing this train makes eventual inclusion much less likely.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin) and host
insights.so_what: Defines the option's expiry: a slip past this fork functionally delays any ETH issuance cut to 2027 or later, extending the current yield regime.

insights.claim: Kevin notes Ethereum's all core devs process has never passed anything with this level of active pushback, that ProgPoW is the precedent for a controversial proposal being killed, and that there has been no major fork of Ethereum since the DAO hard fork.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin)
insights.so_what: Historical precedent tilts toward contentious proposals being shelved rather than forced through, and toward core devs avoiding chain-split risk.
insights.quote: ACD has never really passed something with this level of contentiousness

insights.claim: Kevin predicts all core devs will not push EIP-8363 through without amendments given the volume of dissent, and expects a legislative-style blending of the competing proposals.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin)
insights.so_what: The modal outcome is a softened curve — likely with a nonzero issuance floor — rather than the version currently spooking DeFi.
insights.quote: I don't think that the all core devs are going to push this through if there's this much disscent without amendments.

insights.claim: Kevin stresses that declining to ship an EIP is itself a monetary policy decision, and describes the standoff between core devs and the DeFi constituency as an unstoppable force meeting an immovable object.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin)
insights.so_what: Status quo is not neutral — leaving the current curve in place locks in the drift toward 50%+ staked that the EIP is designed to prevent.
insights.quote: not deciding to do an EIP is a decision in itself

insights.claim: The Ethereum Magicians thread on EIP-8363 accumulated roughly 180-190 comments with the author responding one by one and only through comment 25 at the time of recording.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the governance load; the thread is the primary public venue to monitor for whether the curve gets amended before October.

insights.claim: Jerome argues EIP-8363 is not a significant technical implementation hurdle, so its fate turns purely on social contentiousness rather than engineering maturity — and core devs have historically let contentious discussions continue rather than killing them.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Removes the usual 'too complex to ship in time' escape hatch — the proposal cannot be deferred on technical grounds, only political ones.

insights.claim: Kevin argues there is a genuine zero-sum trade-off between ETH's monetary premium as ultrasound money and its role as a productive asset providing reliable yield for DeFi and institutions, invoking Bankless's triple-point-asset framing of capital asset, consumable asset, and store of value.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin)
insights.so_what: If the trade-off is truly zero-sum, ETH's valuation framework must pick a lane — investors underwriting both a monetary premium and a yield stream may be double-counting.
insights.quote: there's really a zero- sum game between the ultrasound money, uh, vision, which is like monetary premium versus productive asset

insights.claim: Jerome contends ETH remains a productive asset even at a ~45% staking ratio with roughly 0.3% issuance yield, and that a lower risk-free staking rate lets other ETH strategies emerge and compete — explicitly analogized to a central bank cutting its policy rate so other assets become attractive.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Implies a rotation trade inside Ethereum: cutting the protocol 'risk-free' rate should push capital from passive staking into higher-yielding DeFi strategies rather than out of ETH.

insights.claim: Jerome argues that if the only use case for ETH becomes staking, Ethereum would need to completely reconsider its security assumptions and beacon chain design, and that under Lean Ethereum and ZK-EVM a stake-everything equilibrium does not work.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Links the issuance debate to the post-quantum/ZK roadmap — the EF sees rising staking ratios as incompatible with the architecture it intends to ship in three to five years.

insights.claim: Jerome argues sophisticated ETF and DAT investors already dilution-adjust the advertised staking yield and ask where it comes from, so an unaddressed issuance trajectory is itself a problem for the ETH store-of-value narrative.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Directly counters the 'this hurts institutional adoption' claim — the EF believes institutions discount issuance-funded yield, so cutting it may improve rather than harm the pitch.

insights.claim: Grayscale's published research on the issuance debate is described as measured and welcoming of the discussion, in contrast to SharpLink's opposition, with the largest ETH ETF issuers yet to take a public position.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Institutional opinion is not monolithic; a coordinated ETF issuer statement would be the single biggest swing factor and has not happened yet.

insights.claim: Oshene argues institutional investors demand predictability and security above yield, and that issuance changes lack the multi-year telegraphing that gave proof-of-stake and the post-quantum roadmap their social legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Frames process legitimacy, not the yield number, as the institutional risk — a rushed issuance change could cost more in credibility than it saves in dilution.
insights.quote: predictability they want to see something telegraphed for years

insights.claim: Jerome argues Ethereum must decide whether ETH is money and pristine collateral, and that if it cannot, the network would be better off designing a fully dedicated system and solving decentralization separately.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Signals the EF views this as an identity-defining fork in the roadmap, not a parameter tweak — raising the odds of a repeat fight even if this EIP fails.

themes.theme: Solo stakers, taxes, and LST centralization

insights.claim: Jerome, a solo staker since genesis, says his 2.5% yield is a taxable event at France's 30% flat rate and is further eroded by ~1% dilution, so a solo staker's true reservation yield is reached quickly on a tax- and dilution-adjusted basis.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Headline ETH staking APR overstates real economics for taxable holders — the effective net yield today is already close to 0.7-1% for a French solo staker.

insights.claim: Jerome explicitly concedes EIP-8363 will not save solo stakers and that the EF did a poor job initially implying otherwise, arguing only that the proposed curve leaves a better end state than the status quo.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Removes the solo-staker-protection argument from the pro-EIP case; the honest framing is 'less bad', which is a weaker basis for pushing a contentious change.
insights.quote: it's it's not going to save the solar stickers

insights.claim: Jerome argues the status quo is worse for solo stakers because a continuing climb toward 58% staked would drive them out anyway while leaving issuance at roughly 1.1%, producing both fewer solo stakers and higher dilution.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: The comparison that matters is EIP-8363 versus the status-quo trajectory, not versus today's conditions — both paths shed solo stakers, only one caps dilution.

insights.claim: Ethereum's validator entry queue has been full since the SEC issued staking guidance in May 2025, with the staking ratio at roughly 35% and no downtrend, because non-staking holders are incentivized to stake to escape dilution.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: A self-reinforcing flywheel: dilution drives staking, which drives more dilution — this is the mechanism the EIP targets and a reason the 50%-by-2028 forecast is credible.
insights.quote: the entry queue has been full uh since the SEC gave its guidance in May 2025

insights.claim: Oshene calculates that on almost any assumed ratio and equilibrium a staker is better off delegating than solo staking, because solo stakers are taxed as income continuously while wrapped LST holders defer to capital gains at sale.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Tax treatment, not issuance, is the dominant centralizing force pushing ETH into LSTs and custodians — a policy variable outside protocol control.
insights.quote: you're almost always better off delegating except maybe in this worst case scenario where your delegator gets slashed

insights.claim: Oshene points to the Proof of Stake Alliance's US policy push to tax staking rewards as created property taxed at sale — a baker is not taxed when he bakes bread, only when he sells it — as a higher-leverage fix than adjusting the issuance curve.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: US tax reclassification of staking rewards would materially change solo-staking economics and LST demand — a policy catalyst worth tracking independently of the EIP.
insights.quote: a baker doesn't pay taxes when he bakes his bread, he pays it when he sells the bread

insights.claim: Jerome says MEV burn and anti-correlation penalties, not the issuance curve, are what can actually save solo stakers by giving small validators the same competitive economics as large operators who can play timing games for better MEV returns.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: MEV burn is the complementary EIP to watch; both sides agree it matters, and Oshene argues it should ship before any issuance cut.

insights.claim: Oshene sequences the roadmap differently: ship MEV burn first, then reconsider issuance once real-time proving and ZK-EVM cost structures are known, arguing EIP-8363 is simply too early.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: The 'not now' argument is the most likely landing zone if core devs defer — expect issuance to be revisited alongside a post-quantum or ZK fork instead.
insights.quote: I think we should ship Mev burn and you know we should consider this

insights.claim: Oshene rejects an enshrined liquid staking token because any LST must delegate to operators and there is no perfect point in that trade-off space, making a single homogeneous shared-risk token a non-starter.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Damps expectations that an enshrined LST will solve Ethereum's staking concentration; incumbent LSTs face no protocol-level displacement.

insights.claim: Oshene argues the real driver of LST and exchange staking centralization is exit illiquidity — best case about four days to withdraw, currently potentially months with bottlenecked and bank-run-prone queues — not the staking ratio.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Reframes staking centralization as a liquidity problem; any protocol change that shortens exit times would be more bullish for decentralized staking than issuance tweaks.
insights.quote: At the best case scenario, it takes about four days to get your money back. And right now, it well, sorry, it could be months.

insights.claim: Oshene's alternative proposal is a protocol-native instant exit: pay a burn price to withdraw stake immediately, cheap in normal times and priced near the cost to borrow ETH for the queue length, rising under stress.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: A concrete competing EIP concept that would let risk-conscious stakers self-custody instead of using LSTs or exchanges — watch whether it gets formalized as a rival proposal.
insights.quote: the like most credibly neutral thing the protocol could do is have a price to burn a certain amount of ETH and get your stake out of there

insights.claim: Host reports that some solo stakers have said they will exit if ETH yield falls to 2% or lower, and that a projected drop toward 0.3% would likely eliminate the solo staking category and push stakers into ETFs and custodians.
insights.speaker: host (Laura Shin)
insights.so_what: The centralization second-order effect: a yield cut could raise custodial and ETF share of staked ETH, worsening the Nakamoto coefficient the EIP claims to protect.

themes.theme: Chain competition and the future cost model

insights.claim: Jerome argues high headline yields on competing proof-of-stake chains — Solana's roughly 7%+ institutional staking yield — reflect the need to subsidize expensive hardware and server requirements, while Ethereum solo staking runs on hardware costing only hundreds.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Cross-chain yield comparisons are not like-for-like; the cost of running validating infrastructure should be netted out before treating Solana's yield as a competitive threat to ETH.

insights.claim: Jerome notes Bitcoin is now printing less than Ethereum, a reversal from the past, and treats closing that gap as part of the case for the issuance cut.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: The ultrasound-money framing has a concrete comparative: ETH currently loses the hard-money contest to BTC on issuance, a talking point for the sound-money camp.
insights.quote: Bitcoin is printing less than than Epher.

insights.claim: Kevin frames the competitive question as two incompatible investor lenses: the alt-L1 view that all yield is fungible so capital should chase the highest rate, versus the Ethereum view that ETH is a differentiated asset because it is the only network with 100% uptime and multi-client-validated block space.
insights.speaker: Kevin (founder, Gitcoin)
insights.so_what: Which frame institutions actually apply determines whether a lower ETH yield causes outflows to higher-yield chains or is absorbed as the price of pristine settlement.
insights.quote: institutions are choosing Ethereum and ETH because it's the only network with 100% uptime and with this pristine block space that is validated by multiple clients

insights.claim: Oshene argues Ethereum is a couple of hard forks from real-time proving and post-quantum signatures, which will make proposing blocks require a server rack of expensive GPUs and more costly attestation, so today's cost model is not the one issuance should be sized for.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Cutting issuance now against today's cheap cost base risks underfunding a materially more expensive validator set within a few years.
insights.quote: we're a couple hard forks away from real-time proving and a switch to postquantum Ethereum

insights.claim: Oshene estimates post-ZK block production will cost around $100,000 a year in depreciating hardware, warning that under a near-zero issuance regime only about two companies would absorb that cost and produce blocks.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: A concrete centralization forecast with a dollar figure — if correct, the endgame validator set is duopolistic without protocol subsidy, which is the strongest long-run argument against a zero floor.
insights.quote: my math is at something around a 100 grand a year in depreciating hardware to produce blocks when we go that way

insights.claim: Oshene argues the right move learned from the 2024 issuance fight is to build consensus for years and attach an issuance change to a legitimate occasion — post-quantum or real-time ZK proofs — rather than proposing it standalone.
insights.speaker: Oshene (CEO, DV Labs)
insights.so_what: Predicts the eventual shape of a successful issuance change: bundled with an architectural fork, likely 2029-era, not a standalone 2026 EIP.

insights.claim: Jerome says the 0.5% issuance figure is what the Ethereum Foundation protocol team — mostly Justin Drake, by his own account — believes is committable on an ultra-long-term basis under Lean Ethereum, which he describes as a couple of years away.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: The security floor rests on a narrow set of researchers' judgment, which is precisely the legitimacy gap critics are attacking.

insights.claim: Jerome's core timing argument is that the window for a smooth transition is closing: three years from now, when protocol duties change, there will be far more ETH staked and far more entrenched businesses depending on the yield, making the change politically impossible.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: Explains why the EF is willing to absorb a contentious fight now — and implies that if the EIP is deferred, the constituency defending the yield only grows stronger.
insights.quote: we have a window of opportunity for a smooth transition. Um and we should we should not let it close.

insights.claim: Jerome's summary principle for Ethereum monetary policy is to pay stakers as much as necessary but as little as possible to avoid diluting holders, accepting a 45% staking ratio at ~0.3% yield as an acceptable landing zone.
insights.speaker: Jerome (EIP-8363 co-author)
insights.so_what: A clear statement of the EF's objective function: minimize security spend subject to a floor — a durable directional bias toward lower ETH issuance regardless of this EIP's fate.
insights.quote: let's continue to pay stakers as much as necessary but as little as possible so we don't dilute the orders
